extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, instrument-makers, anatomists, and astronomers (readers of Philosophical Transactions, 17th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Composing detailed observational reports and short treatises on instruments, anatomy, optics, astronomy, and related experimental findings in natural philosophy. Emphasises experimental description, instrument construction, observations, and claimed uses or explanations of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetical cylinder construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of Napier's rods, the author writes the numbers on narrow slips of paper, pasted lengthwise on a cylinder of wood or pasteboard, having some small knobs on the surface, by means of which the cylinder is turned round, and thus the arithmetical calculation is performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design criterion for a calculating instrument: numbers on longitudinal slips around a rotatable cylinder; knobs to turn; intended as a practical, mechanical way to perform arithmetical calculations analogous to Napier's rods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refraction proportionality (rule of thumb up to 30°)
rubrics_metrics.description: The refraction of a visual ray in glass, to 30 degrees of inclination, is proportional to the inclination, as far as sense can judge. Where the inclination not exceeding 30°, the angle of refraction of the ray which enters into glass is about a third of the angle of inclination; but the angle of refraction of the ray issuing out of the glass into the air is about half of the angle of its inclination in the glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical rule for optic calculations/expectations within modest angles (≤30°); explicitly stated as perceptual/sensible judgment rather than precise law—useful as practical guidance when designing or reasoning about lenses and telescopes in the absence of precise theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a comprehensive telescope treatise
rubrics_metrics.description: The work is divided into three principal parts: (1) doctrine of optics and dioptrics (refraction, simple vision, refracted vision); (2) theory of the telescope in all its kinds (history of invention, differences ancient vs modern); (3) the positive and mechanical: actual construction of telescopes, their uses, and methods of forming and polishing glasses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing a treatise on telescopes, include foundational optics, a survey/history and typology of telescope kinds, and detailed practical/mechanical sections covering construction, uses, and glass-making/polishing techniques (the mechanical section subdivided into several concrete sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue of telescope-enabled astronomical discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerates major discoveries made by telescopes: conjunction of Mercury with the sun; Venus phases; lunar surface like earth with mountains and libration; sunspots; four satellites of Jupiter; a satellite of Saturn and rings; belts and spots on planets; the Milky Way as innumerable small stars; differences in eclipse timing and apparent size with naked eye vs telescope; Pleiades containing many more stars; Orion having many more stars; observations of many new stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a checklist of phenomena that demonstrate the usefulness of telescopes in celestial observations — a list of observational targets and phenomena to confirm instrument efficacy and scientific value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria to distinguish plant veins from pores/fibres
rubrics_metrics.description: Veins are not pores of the ligneous body or fibres: they are distinct vessels observable in transverse cuts, found in the pith and often in the cortical body, not included within the common tunicle of fibres; the milky juice rises beside and not in any fibre; their course is by the length of the plant; where there is no pith there are none (e.g., roots and trunks), and they are chiefly in the bark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical diagnostic criteria and experiments: (a) examine transverse cuts for distinct vessels separate from fibres; (b) trace juice along length (e.g., dried fennel-stalk dissection); (c) ligature experiments: cutting/dissecting veins causes milky juice to discharge into parenchyma and appear at the ligature; (d) comparative anatomy across species and developmental stages to infer universality and function (carry nutritive succus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based inference of vein functions and ubiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is probable these vessels are in all plants; where not visible they may be present in some parts at certain times; primary use is to carry the succus nutritius of plants (areas without them show no vegetation), secondary use is as the source of vegetable drugs (the 'rich furniture of our shops').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer function and distribution from correlation of presence with vegetation activity and from extraction of characteristic juices; recommend further seasonal and comparative observations and dissections to map position, order, capacity, and differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking-trumpet design principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations on the nature of sounds and how the organ conveys them include: (1) a small tube does not at all magnify sounds; (2) the diameter of the least end must be equal to, if not greater than, the diameter of the speaker's mouth—deficiency reduces magnification; (3) the instrument must be enlarged by degrees and not too suddenly; (4) the mouthpiece must be applied and adapted so that no air or breath is lost while allowing free opening and shutting of the mouth to preserve articulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical design rules for constructing speaking-trumpets: match small-end aperture to mouth size, use gradual flare, ensure mouthpiece fit to prevent air leakage but preserve articulation; these rules are tied to acoustic reasoning and empirical trials (including large trial at Deal Castle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses and operational guidance for speaking trumpet
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported uses: enabling ships to communicate at distances of half a mile to several miles (depending on wind); enabling a single ship's officer to give orders across the deck in storms; admiral to give orders to whole fleet in calm; conveyance of orders from sea-fort to ships; in sieges to communicate ciphered intelligence over miles; a general to address his army; herald to proclaim to many thousands; overseer to direct many hundreds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cases and situational guidance: deploy for long-range spoken communication at sea and land where conventional voice fails; account for wind/direction; combine with signals when reciprocal wind conditions differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical observation and measurement practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Usement of a tube of 13½ feet with convex lenses and a very exact Townley's micrometer; repeated observations should be consistent (author reports repeated observations never differed 20'', very seldom 1/10); confirm observations by comparing with previous observers (Gascoigne, Townley); present tables of longitudes, latitudes, magnitudes, and measured minute distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instrument specification (long focal-length tube, precision micrometer), emphasis on repeated measurements for internal consistency, cross-validation with independent observers, and publishing quantitative tables (coordinates and separations) with stated precision and potential recommended adjustments (e.g., author would advance longitudes several minutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive/diagnostic criteria for mineral balsam (naphtha-like)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed balsam: limpid and of a white colour like the white of an egg, somewhat oleaginous, floating upon all sorts of liquors like oil; cavities contained grains concreted of the liquor resembling 'white amber'; upon chemical distillation the same odour as the balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory and simple chemical (distillation) tests to identify and characterise mineral balsam; notes include claimed medicinal efficacy (applied to the uterus) which motivated its extraction—document source rock, cavities, and physical properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermally reversible salt behavior observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A very white salt extracted from a metallic substance, upon the gentlest heat, resolved into a golden-coloured liquor which, when removed from warmth and exposed to cool air or opening the container, rapidly reformed into the same salt and, while fluid, congealed into very fine threads that extended across the glass like the subtilest cobwebs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record detailed thermal behavior and morphological changes during heating and cooling; note the formation of delicate thread-like solids upon cooling—document preparation and handling as these properties are striking and unusual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental approach to light, colours, and rainbow explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Light is examined experimentally: propagation not only direct/refraction/reflection but also by diffraction; diffusion possibly not instantaneous; colours can be produced by reflection, refraction, diffraction, or intrinsic modification of light; rainbow primary produced by rays once reflected within drops and secondary by rays twice reflected—both involving refraction and reflection by drops and reaching the eye on the axis of the rainbow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiments to test propagation modes (including diffraction), consider temporal aspects (non-instantaneous but imperceptible), analyze colour generation from multiple mechanisms, and explain macroscopic phenomena like rainbows by combining refraction and reflection in drops—support philosophical claims with experimental demonstrations and reasoned ratiocination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for ancient and modern galley (trireme) construction and seating
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatise covers the origin of shipping (oars→sails→both), distinctions between monocrota (single-level oars) and polycrota (multiple tiers), measures such as interscalmium (space between two oars of same row), and methods for placing rowers so that those behind can move under the seat in front—claimed inventions reduce required internal height (three lateral rowers requiring 13½ feet by one method may occupy only 7½ feet by improved placement); another invention claims space for almost half the number of rowers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and ergonomic criteria for war-ships: consider historian/typology, inter-oar spacing, practical arrangements to reduce vessel height and stow more rowers, and conversion between measures (Roman/great/modern feet and cubit) when reconstructing or evaluating historical claims and models.
